blocks.text: Open the compass app on a Tecno or Infinix phone in Lagos and the needle settles toward magnetic north — until you hold the phone near a motorcycle ignition coil or a loudspeaker. The needle swings because every magnet and every current-carrying wire fills the space around it with a magnetic field, the same kind of field that the Earth itself produces.

blocks.markdown:
A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet or a current-carrying conductor in which a magnetic force can be detected. We map it with **field lines**.

Outside a magnet the lines leave the **north pole** and enter the **south pole**. They form closed loops: inside the material they run from south back to north. Lines never cross. Where they are close together the field is strong; where they spread out it is weak.

A small plotting compass placed in the field points along the local field line, north-seeking end in the direction of the field.

rows: Lines leave N, curve round through air, enter S
Lines run from N of one into S of the other; field strong in the gap
Lines repel; a neutral point forms on the axis between them
Concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it
Circles threading the loop; nearly straight through the centre
Like a bar magnet: uniform field inside, looping outside from N to S
blocks.caption: Standard field patterns you must be able to sketch. A neutral point is where two fields cancel, so a compass has no preferred direction.

blocks.title: The right-hand grip rule
blocks.text: Straight wire: point your right thumb in the direction of conventional current; your curled fingers give the field circles. Solenoid: curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of the current in the windings; the thumb then points to the north pole of the solenoid.

blocks.markdown:
### Force on a current in a field — the motor principle

A conductor carrying current $I$ in a magnetic field of flux density $B$ experiences a force. This is the **motor effect**: it is how the armature of a d.c. motor, a moving-coil meter and a loudspeaker cone are driven.

The size of the force is

$$F = BIl\sin\theta$$

where $l$ is the length of wire in the field and $\theta$ is the angle between the current and the field. $F$ is a maximum when the wire is perpendicular to $B$ ($\sin 90^\circ = 1$) and zero when the wire is parallel to $B$.

items: Fleming's left-hand rule (motor rule): First finger = Field (N to S), seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force).
The three directions are mutually perpendicular. If any one is reversed, the force reverses.
The SI unit of $B$ is the tesla (T): a field of 1 T produces a force of 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A when $I$ is perpendicular to $B$.

blocks.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor
blocks.prompt: A straight wire of length 0.50 m carries a current of 5.0 A and lies perpendicular to a uniform field of flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the force on the wire.

steps.text: The wire is perpendicular to the field, so θ = 90° and sin θ = 1.
Substitute the values, all already in SI units.
The direction of this 0.50 N force is given by Fleming's left-hand rule, at right angles to both B and I.

blocks.markdown:
### The Earth's magnetic field

The Earth behaves as if a huge bar magnet lay along its axis, with a south magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole — that is why the **north-seeking** end of a compass points north.

- The **magnetic meridian** at a place is the vertical plane containing the Earth's field direction.
- **Angle of declination** (variation) is the angle between the magnetic meridian and the geographic meridian.
- **Angle of dip** (inclination) is the angle the Earth's field makes with the horizontal. Dip is $0^\circ$ on the magnetic equator and $90^\circ$ at the magnetic poles.

Nigeria lies close to the magnetic equator, so a freely suspended needle is almost horizontal here. In the United Kingdom the same needle would dip steeply downward.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Do not mix the two right-hand rules with Fleming's left-hand rule. Grip rules give you the field or the pole; Fleming's left hand gives you the force on a current that is already in a field. For generators (induced current) you will need Fleming's right-hand rule — that is the next lesson. Also write F = BIl only when the wire is perpendicular to B; otherwise keep the sin θ.

points: Magnetic field lines leave north and enter south; they never cross, and they are densest where the field is strongest.
A long straight wire produces concentric circular field lines; a solenoid produces a field like a bar magnet, uniform inside.
Right-hand grip: thumb = current for a straight wire (fingers = field); fingers = current in a solenoid (thumb = north pole).
The motor force is F = BIl sin θ, with direction from Fleming's left-hand rule (Field, Current, Motion).
The Earth's field has declination and dip; dip is zero on the magnetic equator, which runs near Nigeria.
